must_fix: The diagram gate misstates the agreement rule. Keyframe P ('BOTH AGREE? → CONTINUE / HOLD / STOP, else CHECK FOOTAGE') and beat 7's on-screen 'TWO AIs MUST AGREE' imply that every verdict needs agreement. FACTS: STOP only if the judge says STOP AND the coach says bad; a disagreement gives CHECK FOOTAGE. The judge and coach agreed on flag vs no flag in only 9 of 16 sets, yet only 1 set ended as CHECK FOOTAGE, so HOLD and CONTINUE do not need agreement. Redraw the gate as 'STOP NEEDS BOTH · JUDGE STOP + COACH GOOD → CHECK FOOTAGE' and scope beat 7's on-screen line to STOP (e.g. 'TO CALL STOP, TWO AIs MUST AGREE'). Keep the spoken line as locked; beat 11 is already accurate.

personas.why: I stay to see what happens when the two checks disagree. CHECK FOOTAGE makes the diagram worth saving; the school analogy is where my attention dips.
One STOP out of 23 gets me curious, and the camera-angle mistake earns the watch. When the seated row appears, I think we're starting a third example.
I recognise swinging instead of lifting. Once I'm following a hip-angle graph rather than watching the two reps, I've got my takeaway and scroll.
I stop to find out what he did wrong. He tells me it was leg swing; HOW MY AI READS A SET feels like the start of a different reel.
Seeing the same lunge read differently when he turns is a lovely demonstration. I'd send that comparison, but the judge and coach labels pull me away from it.
The hip dot turning into a wave makes this feel like a project I could try. I'd comment FORM for the diagram, especially after seeing a case where the tracker gets fooled.
122° versus 53° gives me a baseline I can read at a glance. I stay for the false positive, but beat 8 sells me the baseline a second time.
I watch for the return to the crunch to see what each judge actually found. Two outputs agreeing on one clip doesn't earn the word 'always'; I wouldn't forward that rule.
The lunge going from STOP to CHECK FOOTAGE is a concrete example I'd send a colleague. It's more useful than the generic advice to use two AIs.
By the split verdict I understand the decision: disagreement means someone reviews the clip. The topper analogy costs another beat without changing that decision.
The green ghost stops my thumb, and the crossed-out STOP wins me back. On returning to the opening image I already know the verdict, so I don't wait for the offer.
The ghost and red gap communicate the problem without narration. The wave asks me to decode the same difference again before anything new happens.
I'm interested in the disagreement path, not just the pose overlay. I'd save the diagram to inspect what each pass sees and when the system declines to judge.
The camera turn is a convincing failure case, and I want to see both verdicts on the crunch. Two passes of Fable on related evidence can still agree and be wrong.
I'd send the side-on versus turned lunge to a client who films sets. I'd add that the camera changed the reading, not the depth; that's more useful than the STOP stamp.
The red stamp makes me pause, and I get 'swinging, not lifting.' At 10 pm the 17-joint readout looks like a lesson; I leave before the AI makes its mistake.

Bring the turned-lunge comparison forward. MAIN can cut from the swing straight to 'But it flagged this lunge too. Watch what happens when I turn.' TRIAL especially needs that payoff early: it opens on the lunge, leaves it for the crunch, then repeats the hook before explaining it.

Cut the HOW card, seated-row detour and topper analogy. Keep one hip-dot-to-wave animation for builders, then get back to the two verdicts. Put model names, tallies and the full schematic in the promised diagram rather than asking viewers to read them in a one-second hold.

End on the decision the footage supports, not 'always make two AIs agree': 'On the crunch, both flagged a problem. On the lunge, they disagreed, so I checked the clip.' Then make the offer concrete: 'Comment FORM for the video coach and diagram.'
